English: The man **who** lives next to us is a waiter.
German: Der Mann, **der** neben uns wohnt, ist Kellner.
note — the bold part is what the card te: The relative pronoun takes the gender of its noun: der Mann → der. Its verb goes to the end of the clause.

English: The woman **who** works here is nice.
German: Die Frau, **die** hier arbeitet, ist nett.
note — the bold part is what the card te: die Frau → die, the subject of arbeitet.

English: The child **who** is playing outside is my son.
German: Das Kind, **das** draußen spielt, ist mein Sohn.
note — the bold part is what the card te: das Kind → das. Commas close the relative clause on both sides.

English: The people **who** live here are friendly.
German: Die Leute, **die** hier wohnen, sind freundlich.
note — the bold part is what the card te: Plural: die, for every gender.

English: I have a friend **who** lives in Spain.
German: Ich habe einen Freund, **der** in Spanien lebt.
note — the bold part is what the card te: einen Freund is the object of habe, but in his own clause he is the subject: der.

English: That is the bus **that** goes to the station.
German: Das ist der Bus, **der** zum Bahnhof fährt.
note — the bold part is what the card te: For things too: der Bus → der, never was.

English: I'm looking for a company **that** repairs computers.
German: Ich suche eine Firma, **die** Computer repariert.
note — the bold part is what the card te: eine Firma → die, the subject of repariert.

English: The flat **that** has a garden is expensive.
German: Die Wohnung, **die** einen Garten hat, ist teuer.
note — the bold part is what the card te: The relative clause sits right after its noun, inside the main clause.

English: A person **who** reads a lot knows a lot.
German: Ein Mensch, **der** viel liest, weiß viel.
note — the bold part is what the card te: der Mensch → der.

English: Is that the bag **that** belongs to you? (one friend)
German: Ist das die Tasche, **die** dir gehört?
note — the bold part is what the card te: die Tasche → die. gehört goes last.

English: The shop assistant **who** helped me was nice.
German: Der Verkäufer, **der** mir geholfen hat, war nett.
note — the bold part is what the card te: In a perfect at the end, the participle comes first, hat last.

English: Where is the stop **that** is next to the bakery?
German: Wo ist die Haltestelle, **die** neben der Bäckerei ist?
note — the bold part is what the card te: die Haltestelle → die.

English: Children **who** read a lot learn fast.
German: Kinder, **die** viel lesen, lernen schnell.
note — the bold part is what the card te: Plural: die.

English: The book **that** is on the table belongs to me.
German: Das Buch, **das** auf dem Tisch liegt, gehört mir.
note — the bold part is what the card te: das Buch → das, the subject of liegt.

English: The man **who** sees me is my neighbour.
German: Der Mann, **der** mich sieht, ist mein Nachbar.
note — the bold part is what the card te: The man does the seeing, so he is the subject: der.

English: The man **whom** I see is my neighbour.
German: Der Mann, **den** ich sehe, ist mein Nachbar.
note — the bold part is what the card te: Now ich sees him: he is the object, so den.

English: The man **(that)** I met yesterday is a waiter.
German: Der Mann, **den** ich gestern kennengelernt habe, ist Kellner.
note — the bold part is what the card te: English can drop whom; German never drops the relative pronoun. Object, so den.

English: The film **that** we saw was boring.
German: Der Film, **den** wir gesehen haben, war langweilig.
note — the bold part is what the card te: der Film is the object of gesehen, so den.

English: The woman **whom** you see is my teacher. (one friend)
German: Die Frau, **die** du siehst, ist meine Lehrerin.
note — the bold part is what the card te: die stays die in the accusative.

English: The book **that** I'm reading is interesting.
German: Das Buch, **das** ich lese, ist interessant.
note — the bold part is what the card te: das stays das in the accusative.

English: Where is the cake **that** I bought?
German: Wo ist der Kuchen, **den** ich gekauft habe?
note — the bold part is what the card te: der Kuchen as the object: den.

English: The novel **that** you recommended to me is great. (one friend)
German: Der Roman, **den** du mir empfohlen hast, ist toll.
note — the bold part is what the card te: der Roman → den, the object of empfohlen.

English: These are the photos **that** I took.
German: Das sind die Fotos, **die** ich gemacht habe.
note — the bold part is what the card te: Plural object: die. German makes photos: Fotos machen.

English: The jacket **that** she ordered is too big.
German: Die Jacke, **die** sie bestellt hat, ist zu groß.
note — the bold part is what the card te: die Jacke → die. zu before an adjective: too.

English: The colleague **whom** I called is coming tomorrow.
German: Der Kollege, **den** ich angerufen habe, kommt morgen.
note — the bold part is what the card te: der Kollege as the object: den.

English: The waiter recommended a wine **that** we didn't know.
German: Der Kellner hat einen Wein empfohlen, **den** wir nicht kannten.
note — the bold part is what the card te: der Wein → den. kannten: the simple past of kennen.

English: The people **whom** we met were nice.
German: Die Leute, **die** wir getroffen haben, waren nett.
note — the bold part is what the card te: Plural: die, as subject or object.

English: The car **that** he repaired is running again.
German: Das Auto, **das** er repariert hat, fährt wieder.
note — the bold part is what the card te: das Auto → das.

English: The shop assistant **whom** I asked didn't know.
German: Die Verkäuferin, **die** ich gefragt habe, wusste es nicht.
note — the bold part is what the card te: die Verkäuferin → die.

English: The waitress **whom** we asked was very kind.
German: Die Kellnerin, **die** wir gefragt haben, war sehr freundlich.
note — the bold part is what the card te: die Kellnerin as the object: die.
